note: The community is told to gather often and seek what benefits souls because even the whole time of faith will not profit if one is not complete at the end; time, gain, and final perseverance converge.

ref: Gregory the Great, Homilies on the Gospels 19
basis: Vineyard hours as ages of life

Paul urges steadfastness and abundance in the Lord's work, knowing that labor is not empty; the commentary's loss versus enduring wage is stated directly.
Paul says the Day reveals each builder's work and tests what sort it is; the commentary's payday includes judgment of the work itself.
Work that survives the test brings its worker a reward; it supplies the positive balance opposite the loss in the adjoining verse.
Paul says a builder whose work burns suffers loss though the person is saved; it distinguishes lost work from lost self in the commentary's final account.
The commentary links work to the wage due; Paul says the planter and waterer are one and each will receive a wage according to labor. It directly connects effort to compensation.
Paul says planter and waterer each receive wages according to their labor; this directly joins the commentary's intentional work and earned payment.
The requirement for a steward is to be found faithful; it supplies a concrete office for the commentary's trust opposed to betrayal.

basis: Paul's reading of the unmuzzled ox

basis: ransom not paid in silver or gold

basis: work of faith, labor of love, endurance of hope

basis: Work of faith and endurance of hope

basis: Patiently admonish and help one another
note: The congregation is urged to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with all; the counsel to patience takes concrete social form.

The commentary says the wage is owed when work is done; in instructions about elders, Paul cites the saying that the worker deserves his wages. It applies the laborer's due to support for community leaders.

The wealthy are urged to store a good foundation for the future and take hold of real life; the commentary's altered investment of wealth has a close analogue.

basis: Nothing brought in, nothing carried out
note: Paul observes that people enter the world with nothing and can take nothing away; the commentary's goods expire at the human boundary.

basis: now is the day of salvation

The commentary calls haqq each person's share and mutual recognition of another's due; Paul says one community's abundance should supply another's need so there may be equality. It turns right share into reciprocal material care.

basis: Sparing or generous sowing and reaping
note: The measure of what one sows determines the harvest in Paul's appeal for a collection; charity is treated as an investment whose return follows its measure.

basis: Lose work or receive full reward
note: The readers are warned to watch themselves so their labor is not lost and they receive a full reward; it binds vigilance, loss, and complete payment.

basis: Good works still prepared for believers

basis: Salvation described as grace through faith
note: The letter says salvation comes by grace through faith as God's gift; it puts a gift frame beside the commentary's wage frame for believing.

basis: Not from works, so no boasting

basis: Work honestly to share with the needy
note: The former thief must work with his hands at what is good so he has something to share with one in need; intentional labor becomes another person's due.

basis: Do good while there is opportunity

basis: Good work and harvest in due season
note: The community must not tire of doing good, because it will reap in due time if it does not give up; good action, patience, and deferred pay meet in one verse.

basis: stir one another to love and good works
note: The commentary makes mutual urging toward truth and patience part of the exception; Hebrews tells hearers to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works. It gives mutual exhortation an explicitly ethical aim.

basis: Provoke one another to good deeds
note: The congregation must consider how to stir one another to love and good works; it is a direct communal form of the commentary's reciprocal exhortation.

basis: encourage one another as the Day approaches
note: The commentary says the market closes on a coming day; Hebrews commands mutual encouragement all the more as the Day draws near. The approaching deadline intensifies communal action.

basis: Encourage more as day draws near
note: The community must keep meeting and encourage one another increasingly as the Day approaches; reciprocal counsel intensifies toward a fixed deadline.

basis: Lost property and better lasting possession

basis: God rewards those who seek him
note: The commentary makes belief one condition of escaping loss and describes a later wage; Hebrews says faith is necessary to approach God and that God rewards those who seek him. It joins faith to expected recompense.

basis: Esau's bargain read as moral warning
note: Hebrews recalls Esau selling his birthright for a single meal to warn against an unholy choice; it interprets Genesis's market exchange as sacrificing a durable inheritance.

The addressees must exhort one another daily while it is called today, lest anyone harden through deceit; mutual counsel has the commentary's passing-time urgency.

basis: Work remembered by a just payer
note: God is not unjust to forget work and love shown in service to the saints; the wage due for good work is backed by divine justice.
The commentary pairs belief with patience and a future wage; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit promises through faith and patience. It makes endurance part of receiving what is promised.
The audience is told to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; two terms of the surah's exception become conditions of deferred receipt.

James concludes that a person is justified by works and not faith alone; it places the commentary's joined belief and work within a specific interpretive dispute.

The commentary treats lifetime as capital spent in exchange; James addresses people planning to travel, trade, and make a profit for a year. The passage puts the trader's plan inside an uncertain lifespan.

The commentary makes wage a due share; James says the wages withheld from field workers cry out and have reached the Lord of hosts. It links labor injustice to divine hearing.

The commentary makes patience the condition of receiving a later wage; James compares patient endurance to a farmer waiting for the precious crop. It gives patience a concrete work-and-harvest scene.
The addressees are told to be patient until the Lord's coming as a farmer waits for precious fruit; deferred yield and endurance meet in a work scene.

basis: patience because the Lord's coming is near
note: The commentary urges mutual patience as the end approaches; James tells hearers to be patient and establish their hearts because the Lord's coming is near. It binds endurance to a closing time.
The audience must also be patient and firm because the Lord's coming is near; it makes the promised settlement, rather than waiting alone, the point.

basis: Reaper receives wage for eternal harvest
note: The reaper already receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life; the commentary's daily worker and final, lasting payment are joined explicitly.

Jesus calls believing in the one God sent the work of God; it ties the commentary's belief and work more tightly than a mere sequence of two acts.

The commentary sets the day worker's labor against the day's end; Jesus says his work must be done while it is day, since night is coming when no one can work. The saying makes the workday a figure for a closing opportunity.
Jesus says work must be done during daylight because night comes when no one can work; this gives the commentary's closing workday a direct moral deadline.

The commentary treats wages as the worker's due; Jesus tells the traveling disciples that the laborer deserves his wages while they stay in a household. It applies the wage-right formula to religious workers.
Jesus instructs envoys to accept a host's provision because the worker deserves wages; the commentary's wage is treated as a right, not a gift.

basis: rich man expects many years of ease
note: The commentary rejects the idea that wealth makes a person outlive time; the rich fool tells his soul to rest because he has goods stored for many years. The speech exposes the assumed conversion of capital into extra life.

basis: Stored goods imagined to buy many years
note: The rich man addresses his soul as having goods stored for many years and plans to rest; it states the precise illusion about wealth and lengthened life corrected in the following verse.
The commentary says a market will close and a person may then ask for more time; God tells the rich fool his life is required that very night. It makes the deadline sudden and non-negotiable.
The rich man's accumulated goods cannot extend the deadline when his life is required that night; this closely meets the commentary's hoarder who thinks property lengthens life.

basis: rich toward God rather than stored wealth
note: The commentary says amassed property cannot make its owner outlive time; Jesus concludes that the person who stores treasure for himself but is not rich toward God is a fool. It gives the alternative to temporal accumulation.

basis: Stored wealth and poverty toward God
note: The parable concludes that storing for oneself leaves one poor toward God; it supplies the distinction between a full earthly account and lasting gain.

basis: selling goods to give alms and store unfailing treasure
note: The commentary presents a trade whose return does not fail and recalls a plea for time to give charity; Jesus tells hearers to sell possessions, give to the poor, and provide an unfailing heavenly treasure. It makes generosity a deliberate transfer from perishable wealth.

basis: Sell goods for an unfailing purse
note: Jesus directs hearers to sell possessions and give alms, making a purse that does not grow old; diminishing earthly goods can yield lasting treasure.

The commentary links righteous deeds to a later wage; Jesus says a host who invites the poor, disabled, lame, and blind will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous. It specifies generosity that cannot be repaid in the present market.

The commentary glosses trust as the opposite of betrayal; Jesus says faithfulness in little predicts faithfulness in much, and dishonesty in little predicts dishonesty in much. The next verse applies this to money, making trust a test of stewardship.
The person faithful in very little is faithful in much; the commentary's trust in dealings applies to small transactions before a greater settlement.

basis: faithfulness with money and true riches
note: The commentary sets trust against betrayal in a commercial setting; Jesus says that failure to be faithful with unrighteous wealth means no one will entrust true riches. It makes money management a test of trustworthiness.
Jesus asks who will entrust true riches to those unfaithful with worldly wealth; handling temporary capital becomes a test of entrusted responsibility.
Jesus asks who will give the stewards their own if they have not been faithful with someone else's; entrusted capital is the test for lasting possession.

basis: God and wealth as rival masters
note: The commentary frames the righteous trade as choosing the lasting good over a losing exchange; Jesus says a person cannot serve both God and mammon. It makes wealth a question of allegiance, not merely its amount.

The commentary makes business an account whose capital can be lost; the rich man in Jesus' parable demands an account from a steward accused of squandering his property. It makes stewardship answerable before the owner.

The commentary says the final day has no market in which to act or settle accounts; in the rich man and Lazarus story a fixed gulf prevents passage after death. It pictures the irreversibility of the closed opportunity.

The commentary asks whether capital is spent on a durable return; Jesus tells disciples to use worldly wealth in a way that may welcome them into eternal dwellings. The link is a deliberate investment whose payoff exceeds the market.

basis: Use passing wealth for enduring welcome
note: Jesus says to make friends by means of unrighteous wealth so they receive one into eternal dwellings when it fails; finite capital can be spent for an enduring return.

The commentary makes the market open only for a limited time; the nobleman tells servants to conduct business with the entrusted money until he returns. The parable makes the interval before return a period of accountable investment.
A nobleman gives money to servants and orders them to do business until he comes back; the commentary's market stays open for a limited absence.

The commentary imagines an account closing after a period of work; on returning, the nobleman summons the servants to learn what each gained in trade. The scene makes the yield of entrusted capital reviewable.
At his return the owner summons the servants to learn what they gained by trading; it is a direct closing of the ledger after elapsed time.
The giver receives a good, pressed, overflowing measure, and the measure used is returned; it reworks the commentary's short measure into ample recompense.
Jesus asks what a person gains by winning the whole world but losing or forfeiting oneself; it is especially close to the commentary's gloss that the ultimate loss is the person.

basis: profit of the world, loss of the self
note: The commentary says the ultimate loss is the person and family; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life. The saying puts market gain directly against losing the self.
Jesus asks what it profits a person to gain the whole world and forfeit life; the commentary's losing capital ultimately means losing the self.

basis: merchant buys the pearl of great value
note: The commentary presents faith and righteous action as a better trade; Jesus' merchant sells all he has to buy one pearl of great value. The parable gives costly exchange a positive, kingdom-directed outcome.
The merchant sells all he has to buy the uniquely valuable pearl; surrendering capital becomes a successful transaction, beside the commentary's saving trade.

basis: Worldly gain cannot compensate a soul
note: Jesus asks what profit gaining the world has if one forfeits life and what could be given in exchange; it repeats the commentary's ultimate calculation of self-loss in another Gospel setting.
The Son of Man will come in glory and repay each person according to what each has done; the self-loss question in the preceding verse is followed by the work account.

basis: Sell holdings and give poor for heavenly treasure
note: Jesus tells a wealthy man to sell his possessions and give to the poor to have treasure in heaven; another person's need converts current capital into enduring value.

basis: Leaving family and property for life
note: Jesus promises a manifold return and eternal life to followers who leave family or fields for his name; it turns loss of family and holdings, disastrous in the commentary's quoted warning, into a chosen cost with promised return.

basis: workers protest equal pay for unequal hours
note: The commentary speaks of the due wage for labor; the first-hired workers protest that the one-hour workers were made equal to them after they bore the day's heat. The complaint exposes the tension between measured effort and equal payment.

basis: One hour versus full day's labor
note: The late workers have worked only one hour, while others bore the whole day's burden; the contrast sharpens the commentary's question of time spent and recompense.

basis: agreed denarius as a worker's due
note: The commentary says a wage is an obligation once due; the vineyard owner answers a complaint by pointing to the agreed denarius. This gives the parable's wage a contractual basis alongside its generosity to later workers.

basis: Agreed wage owed to the worker
note: The owner tells the complaining worker he has fulfilled the agreed denarius; this specifies the commentary's wage as a settled contractual right.

The owner appeals to his right to use his own money generously; the text complicates the commentary's strict wage ledger with unmeasured gift.

basis: Agreed denarius for a day's work
note: The vineyard owner agrees with laborers on a denarius for the day before sending them out; it sets the contracted amount whose evening distribution drives the story.

The commentary's day laborer reaches the wage deadline at the day's end; in Jesus' vineyard parable the owner orders the workers called and paid when evening comes. The scene directly joins a day's labor to its wage.
The commentary's afternoon laborer reaches payday as the day ends; the vineyard owner calls the workers at evening to receive wages, making the daily deadline concrete.
The workers hired at the eleventh hour receive a denarius; payment after little remaining daylight complicates any simple equation of duration and wage.

basis: Door closes while buyers are away
note: While the unprepared bridesmaids go to buy oil, the bridegroom arrives and the door shuts; the commentary's market closure becomes a concrete missed final opportunity.

basis: Unknown day and hour require watch
note: The parable closes by telling hearers to watch because the day and hour are unknown; the closed door has an unknowable rather than negotiable deadline.
The first servant trades the master's five talents and makes five more; the commentary's believer as faithful trader has a concrete scene.

basis: settling accounts after a long time
note: The commentary says capital is spent as time passes; in the talents parable the master returns after a long time and settles accounts with the servants entrusted with money. It links investment, delay, and reckoning.
After a long time, the master returns to reckon with servants entrusted with talents; passing time and entrusted capital end in an account.

The commentary connects faithful work to a wage; the master praises a servant faithful over a little, entrusts him with much, and invites him into joy. It adds increased responsibility as the reward for stewardship.
The master calls the profitable servant good and faithful and sets him over more; profitable dealing is judged as trustworthiness.

basis: money placed with bankers for interest
note: The commentary describes capital invested for gain; in the talents parable the master says the servant should have placed the money with bankers so it could return with interest. It makes the expected return explicit.
The master says the idle servant should have placed his money with bankers so it returned with interest; merely preserving the principal fails the investment test.

basis: service to the least counted as service to the king
note: The commentary says mutual counsel must recognize another person's due; in the judgment scene the king identifies care for the least of his siblings as care for himself. It gives acts of service a direct relation to the final judge.

basis: Deeds toward least count toward king
note: The king treats care for the least of his brothers as done to himself; another person's due becomes part of the worker's final assessment.

basis: treasure consumed by moth and rust
note: The commentary warns that what one owns is used up; Jesus says earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth, rust, and thieves. It supplies a concrete image of stored capital that cannot be secured.

Treasure kept in heaven is beyond moth, rust, and thieves; it answers the commentary's contrast between exhausted human holdings and what endures with God.

The commentary distinguishes a losing trade from the profitable exchange of faith and deeds; Paul says what had been gain he now counts as loss because of Christ. The passage reverses the account's valuation, making apparent profit a loss.
Paul counts what had been gains as loss for Christ; it gives the commentary's profit-and-loss vocabulary a deliberate reversal of value.
Paul accepts the loss of all things to gain Christ; the text distinguishes chosen material loss from the commentary's ruinous loss of self.

basis: Gift produces credit in the giver's account
note: Paul says he seeks fruit increasing to the donors' account rather than the gift itself; generosity becomes an accumulating return in the commentary's moral ledger.

basis: another person stands behind a debt
note: The commentary's lexical branch calls sabīr a guarantor; Paul tells Philemon to charge any debt or wrong by Onesimus to Paul's own account. It gives the guarantor image a concrete personal act of bearing another's liability.

basis: faithful through death, crowned with life

basis: reward according to each person's work
note: The commentary presents a wage arriving after a period of labor; the returning Christ says he brings recompense to repay each according to work. It makes the final wage explicit.

basis: Buy refined gold from the speaker
note: The speaker counsels a materially self-satisfied church to buy gold from him so it becomes rich; true capital is defined against apparent wealth.

basis: people purchased for God by blood

God repays every person according to deeds; the commentary's final wage uses an individual account of actual work.

basis: Persistence in good work seeks immortality

basis: Arabic root ء م ن; package table's unverified sound correspondence to Hebrew/Aramaic אמנ

basis: Calculate loss of a good deed against reward
note: The saying instructs a person to reckon a commandment's apparent loss against its reward and a transgression's apparent gain against its loss; it articulates the commentary's moral profit calculation.

basis: Day short, work great, wage great

basis: The grave does not cancel accounting

basis: Give to a friend before death
